title: "Boards and constraints"

**`@board`: pin assignments and the constraint files**

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
using QuartzHDL
using QuartzHDL.Units
```

The design says nothing about pins, and the board says nothing about logic. A `@board` is the pin map of one physical board; the constraint files are written from the two together, and refuse if they disagree.

## `@board`

```{julia}
#| output: false
@quartz struct Top
  @in  rst::Bool = false  active=:low
  @out led::Bits{4} = 0
  @io  sda::Pad{1} = Pad{1}(:pullup)
  n::Bits{26} = 0
end

@on Top posedge(clk) begin
  @reset(rst)
  n ← n + 1
  led ← n[22:25]
end

@wire Top sda ← release()

@board Rev2 begin
  "revision 2 of the evaluation board"
  device  = "LFE5U-25F-6BG381C"
  io      = :LVCMOS33                  # every pin below, unless it says otherwise

  clk => (pin="G2", osc=12MHz)         # a rate belongs with the pin it arrives on
  rst => (pin="R1", pull=:up)
  sda => (pin="T2", drive=8, ext_pull=:up)
  led => (pins=["A9", "B9", "A10", "B10"], io=:LVCMOS25)
end
```

Every line is either a setting — `key = value` — or a binding of a port to its pin. Ports are named as the design names them; the constraint file names the pins as the emitted Verilog does. A port of an instance is addressed by path, `uart.tx`. A site is written the way the datasheet writes it: `"G2"` on a BGA, `pin = 27` on a numbered package.

A setting that is a pin attribute (`io`, `pull`, `ext_pull`, `drive`) applies to every binding; a binding overrides it, `nothing` included — `(pin=27, io=nothing)` says "left to the tool, on purpose". `pins=[...]` takes `nothing` for a bit with no pin, and an attribute may vary by bit: `pull=(0:2 => :down,)`.

Two of those are pulls, and they say who provides one. `pull` is the FPGA's own weak pull, configured in the bitstream, so it goes into the constraint file. `ext_pull` is a resistor on the board: it goes nowhere, but it is how the board says a net is pulled without the FPGA's help. A pad that relies on a pull — `Pad{1}(:pullup)` in the design, which is what its [simulation](wires.qmd) models — must get one from the board, either way; that is checked when the constraint file is written.

Attribute names are a closed set, checked where they are written, since a misspelt one that was quietly ignored would leave a pin with the wrong buffer. A string at the top documents the board; one before a binding documents the pin.

## `LPF`: the constraint file

```{julia}
write(stdout, Top, LPF(Rev2));
```

`LPF` writes the Lattice constraint file: pin sites, buffer settings, the frequency of every clock the logic runs on (from the oscillators and the clock tree, through every black box), the nets that want a global buffer, and the timing exceptions — one for every source and sink of a [`Multicycle`](multicycle.qmd) wire, and any declared by hand with `@multicycle`.

Which clocks ride the chip's global distribution is a choice about the design, made once on the top module:

```julia
@primary Top clk, clk_fast
```

Each name must be a clock the design has, and `LPF` writes a `USE PRIMARY NET` line for each. A design that says nothing leaves the choice to the tool.

A clock that arrives on a pin needs care, because synthesis puts a buffer behind the pin and names the net after it `clk_i_c`: a constraint on the net `clk_i` would match nothing, and the tool would drop it with only a warning. So its frequency is written against the port, `FREQUENCY PORT "clk_i"`, and its global buffer against the buffered net, `USE PRIMARY NET "clk_i_c"` — the name Synplify gives it, the synthesiser a [Diamond workspace](compiling.qmd) uses. A clock that nothing runs on, such as one only [read as data](blackbox.qmd), gets no frequency line, since there is no logic for it to time.

## `QSF` and `SDC`: the Quartus files

A part Quartus builds for, such as a MAX 10 or a Cyclone, takes two files, because Quartus keeps settings apart from timing. `QSF` writes the settings: the family and the device, the pin of every port, the I/O standard, weak pull-up and drive strength of each, and a global clock assignment for every net named by `@primary`. A board-wide `io` also becomes the device's default standard, which sets the voltage of the banks no port lands in; without it Quartus supplies those at 2.5 V, and warns when the configuration pins then sit across two voltages. Quartus also warns of an output with no `drive`, so a board gives its outputs one, from the drives the standard allows on that part; on a MAX 10 the 3.3 V LVCMOS standard allows only 2 mA, and an LED wants LVTTL. `SDC` writes the timing constraints: a `create_clock` for every clock the logic runs on, and for every multicycle path a setup exception of N cycles paired with a hold exception of N-1, which is where Quartus expects the hold check to stay.

```{julia}
@board Kit begin
  "the MAX 10 10M08S evaluation kit"
  device = "10M08SAE144C8G"
  io     = :LVCMOS33

  clk => (pin=27, osc=50MHz)
  rst => (pin=120, ext_pull=:up)
  sda => (pin=74, ext_pull=:up)
  led => (pins=[132, 134, 135, 140])
end

write(stdout, Top, QSF(Kit));
write(stdout, Top, SDC(Kit));
```

The board is written the same way whichever vendor made the part. The device decides which files it takes: `LPF` refuses a part Quartus builds for, and `QSF` and `SDC` refuse any other, so a board cannot be given to the wrong tool by mistake. Two attributes have a vendor's flavour. An I/O standard is written as `:LVCMOS33` and spelt for Quartus as `"3.3-V LVCMOS"`; a standard QuartzHDL has no spelling for is given as a string in Quartus's own words, `io = "3.3-V SCHMITT TRIGGER"`. And these parts have no weak pull-down, so `pull = :down` is refused on them; a resistor on the board is `ext_pull = :down` on any part.

## What they refuse

The constraint writers check the design against the board and refuse to write anything if:

- a port has no pin, or a pin names a port that does not exist;
- two ports sit on one site;
- a port's width does not match its pin count;
- a pad relies on a pull and the board provides none, neither `pull` nor `ext_pull`, or pulls the other way;
- a black box that makes a clock sits below the top module, where the constraints cannot reliably name its clocks (see [black boxes](blackbox.qmd)).

```{julia}
#| error: true
@board Wrong begin
  device = "LFE5U-25F-6BG381C"
  clk => (pin="G2", osc=12MHz)
  rst => (pin="R1")
  led => (pins=["A9", "B9", "A10"])   # three pins for a 4-bit port
  sda => (pin="T2")                   # and no pull-up for an open-drain pad
end
write(devnull, Top, LPF(Wrong))
```

Each of those would otherwise be found only on the board.

::: {.callout-tip title="If you know Verilog"}
`@board` plus `LPF`, or `QSF` and `SDC`, replaces the hand-maintained `.lpf` or `.qsf` and `.sdc` and keeps them in step with the design: rename a port, and the constraint line follows; add a `Multicycle` wire, and its exception appears. Lattice's and Quartus's formats are written today; the `@board` description itself holds nothing vendor-specific except the device name and the spelling of an I/O standard given as a string.
:::

## The command line

```
quartz design.jl --top Top --board Rev2 --outdir build
quartz design.jl --top Top --board Kit --outdir build
```

writes `Top.v` and `Rev2.lpf` together, or `Top.v`, `Kit.qsf` and `Kit.sdc`, which is what a build script calls.
